transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-20
Time: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~48 mins
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Newton Harbor SRE), Liam O'Connor (Head of Cloud), Sara Mitchell (Legal), Tom Reyes (Data Governance)

Summary (auto):
Quick discovery focused on private/VPC onramp, geo-data residency constraints, and egress/policy requirements. Newton Harbor wants to evaluate Redwood Private with transit gateway peering and guaranteed egress IPs; discussed Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs for latency/cost. Agreed on pilot and baseline tests; next steps assigned.

Topics:
- VPC peering vs Transit Gateway patterns
- Private endpoints (privatelink) and DNS leakage
- Egress IP allocation and IP slicing for multi-tenant routing
- Regional restrictions / data residency / legal review
- KMS/HSM & audit logs

Action items (briefed): see action_items field

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we're Jordan from Redwood, AE, and Miguel from the SE team. How is everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Desai: Good, thanks. We got a packed agenda; want to make sure we cover the onramp and the residency constraints up front.
[00:12] Jordan Kim: Perfect. At a high level can you run us through current infra and what success looks like for a pilot?
[00:20] Liam O'Connor: Yeah so we run most services in AWS across us-west-2 and eu-west-1. Our primary concern is that model inference for PII containing payloads stays within specific regions and never egresses to third regions. We also need fixed egress IPs for allow-listing with partners, and SSO integration.
[00:36] Miguel Santos: Got it. When you say fixed egress do you mean a small set of static IPs per region or are you expecting per-tenant distinct ranges?
[00:43] Tom Reyes: Ideally per-environment ranges; we can do some CIDR slicing for dev/stage/prod. For production we want a predictable small set of IPs so downstream partners can firewall them.
[00:53] Priya Desai: Also, we use Transit Gateway for our cross-account routing — so the pattern that works for us is TGW attachment from Redwood VPC into our network, or a PrivateLink style endpoint if that's simpler from an ops perspective.
[01:04] Miguel Santos: We support both. There are trade-offs: TGW attachments give you more direct routing and simpler egress control, PrivateLink keeps the traffic entirely via AWS privatelink endpoints but requires endpoint ENIs and DNS config.
[01:16] Jordan Kim: Quick note — sometimes the auto-transcribe here calls PrivateLink 'private link' or 'privet link' so apologies if the transcript mixes up spelling.
[01:22] Sara Mitchell: From legal, we'll need clarity on data at rest and key management. We operate under EU data residency constraints and some customers stipulate that keys are in their control via HSM or customer-managed KMS.
[01:33] Miguel Santos: We have two main private deployment patterns: 1) Redwood Private (customer VPC peering / TGW) where the control plane is in our account but all inference traffic flows over peered/transit connections; 2) On-prem/VPC bundle — we can also package a private control plane you run in your VPC or in a private AWS account for stricter KMS controls.
[01:54] Liam O'Connor: How much extra ops overhead on our side for the second option? Sounds like we might want customer-managed KMS if legal insists on that.
[02:02] Miguel Santos: The customer-managed control plane option adds a bit of setup — we provide an installer and a runbook. You get direct KMS integration and HSM if required, but Redwood will still provide observability hooks. We usually scope that for larger enterprise deals.
[02:13] Priya Desai: Ok networking nitty gritty — for TGW attachment we need account IDs and region list. We also need guidance: do you punch routes via the TGW or use proxy egress from Redwood side?
[02:25] Miguel Santos: Typical pattern is Redwood announces routes and we can NAT/egress from our fleet with a fixed egress IP set. Alternatively, we can enable hairpinning through your TGW so egress remains on your side. Both are supported but differ in SLAs and troubleshooting.
[02:39] Priya Desai: Is there an option for colocated egress per region? Example: US data processed in us-west-2 and egress there; EU in eu-west-1 and never crosses.
[02:48] Jordan Kim: Yes, we can gate by region. The routing policy will honor region pins; we also have a 'region lockdown' feature where requests tagged for EU models are pinned to EU capacity. It's in the rollout for Private.
[02:59] Tom Reyes: DNS concerns — with Privatelink the ENIs create private hostnames, we want to ensure no accidental public DNS resolution or split-horizon leakage.
[03:08] Miguel Santos: You'll need to override the resolver in your VPC or use Route53 inbound endpoints. Also, our client side SDK can be configured to hit the private endpoint. There are a few gotchas with SDKs and CORS if you have browser flows.
[03:20] Liam O'Connor: On the Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoff — our teams did a rough cost calc. Hosted is simpler but we need to be sure PII doesn't transit public networks and the latency is acceptable. Dedicated gives more predictable throughput. Any latency numberballpark?
[03:33] Miguel Santos: For a typical gpt-style 7B open model on g4dn equivalent, p50 latency for 64-token requests is around 40–70ms in region; dedicated reserved pools usually shave another 10–20ms depending on instance type and batching. But perf depends heavily on sequence length and batch behavior.
[03:48] Priya Desai: We send 256–512 token model calls in some cases, so KV cache and streaming behavior matter. Will Redwood support pinned KV cache across requests?
[03:56] Miguel Santos: We do KV cache hinting; for Private deployments we can persist warm contexts in a local cache. That reduces startup token overhead. The term you might see in the docs is 'prefix/K-V cache', sometimes hyphenated in transcripts — apologies for transcription glitches.
[04:09] Sara Mitchell: For compliance, we need logs showing request traceability, per-tenant audit logs, and retention controls. Can you redact request bodies in logs?
[04:18] Jordan Kim: We offer configurable logging levels; you can choose to redact payloads, store only metadata, or keep full request bodies in an encrypted bucket with access controls. We'll include the log retention controls in the security packet.
[04:30] Tom Reyes: Another question — partner allow-listing needs static egress IPs per region. How many IPs do you typically provide?
[04:38] Miguel Santos: We can provide a small set of egress IPs per region per deployment — usually between 3–12 IPs depending on scale and HA topology. If you want per-tenant IP ranges that is doable but increases complexity and likely cost.
[04:50] Priya Desai: Network ACLs: do you support TLS mutual auth with your private endpoint?
[04:55] Miguel Santos: Mutual TLS is supported for certain control channels; for data plane traffic we typically rely on TLS 1.2/1.3 and private network protections, but we can discuss mTLS as a requirement.
[05:05] Liam O'Connor: On the pilot: we want to validate latency, region locking, and egress behavior. Would you be able to run a short POC with our sample corpus then share a CSV of per-request timings and the egress path?
[05:16] Jordan Kim: Yes — Miguel will run the baseline and we'll provide a template for the CSV and the measurement harness.
[05:21] Sara Mitchell: Also legal will need an export of SOC2 type II and Amazon VPC Flow log retention policies if flow logs are used.
[05:28] Jordan Kim: We'll push the SOC2 package and our data processing agreement. We'll flag how KMS integration looks in both hosted and customer-managed options.
[05:35] Tom Reyes: A small wrinkle: some of our customers restrict cross-account peering and prefer an accept-only privatelink model. Is there any limit on number of privatelink endpoints per region?
[05:44] Miguel Santos: AWS limits vary but functionally we can support many endpoints. There's an operational cost per endpoint. We'll call out the limits in the runbook.
[05:51] Priya Desai: Encryption key custody — can Redwood support BYOK with HSM-backed key material stored in our AWS KMS?
[05:58] Miguel Santos: Yes for the customer-managed control plane we can use customer KMS keys; for hosted we use our KMS and can offer envelope encryption with customer-managed root keys in some agreements. We'll note the details in the security artifacts.
[06:11] Liam O'Connor: Any particular blockers you foresee for a quick pilot?
[06:14] Jordan Kim: The usual blockers are network approvals (security team needs CIDR lists), legal review of DPA, and potential limits on Privatelink endpoints.
[06:22] Sara Mitchell: We'll aim to get legal questions back in 48 hours.
[06:25] Priya Desai: We'll gather CIDRs and TGW info; also need list of partner endpoints that require egress allow-listing.
[06:33] Miguel Santos: For the baseline I'll need a small payload sample and an API key — we'll use a dedicated test tenancy that isolates your data; we'll also show how to configure the SDK for private endpoints.
[06:44] Jordan Kim: Quick recap of next steps: Jordan sends the network runbook and security checklist; Miguel runs latency baseline; Newton Harbor shares CIDRs and region whitelist; legal requests SOC2 docs. We'll aim for the POC kickoff next week.
[06:59] Tom Reyes: Sounds good. One last thing — do you have recommended instance types for heavy concurrent low-latency workloads?
[07:05] Miguel Santos: For large concurrency we recommend A100 or equivalent for some models, but for smaller models optimized 4-bit quantized instances on cost-effective GPUs give a sweet spot. We'll include model-specific sizing guidance in the follow-up.
[07:18] Priya Desai: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up internally and come back with the items.
[07:22] Jordan Kim: Thanks all, appreciate it.

End of transcript.
